steps.title: A Bordeaux grape
steps.body: Carmenère was once widely planted in Bordeaux, especially in the Médoc, and valued for its colour. But it suffered from coulure, poor fruit set in cool, wet springs, giving low and irregular yields. After phylloxera destroyed Bordeaux's vineyards in the late 19th century, growers didn't replant it. It almost vanished from France.

steps.title: Chile today
steps.body: In the mid-19th century, Chilean growers brought Bordeaux cuttings, including Carmenère, before phylloxera struck. Chile's dry, warm climate suited it better than Bordeaux's. Today Chile grows about 95% of the world's Carmenère, around 10,000 hectares, especially in Colchagua, Cachapoal, Maipo and Peumo.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Carmenère role.
steps.explanation: Carmenère's map shifted from France to Chile.

steps.title: Elsewhere
steps.body: Small plantings remain in Bordeaux, and some were rediscovered in northern Italy, where they had been mistaken for Cabernet Franc. China also grows a grape called Cabernet Gernischt, now thought to be Carmenère. Some is planted in California and Washington.

steps.prompt: Why did Carmenère almost disappear from Bordeaux?
options: Poor fruit set and phylloxera led growers not to replant it
steps.explanation: Coulure made yields unreliable, so after phylloxera growers replanted other grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carmenère was a Bordeaux grape, lost after phylloxera
Chile grows about 95% of the world's Carmenère
Small plantings survive in Italy, China and Bordeaux
